tagline: Alps, caves and a green heart
overview:
Slovenia packs an astonishing variety into an area smaller than New Jersey. In one day a traveler can ski in the Julian Alps, walk through a cave the size of a cathedral, and swim in the Adriatic Sea, because the country's 47 kilometers of coastline lie only a couple of hours from its northern peaks. Slovenia borders Italy, Austria, Hungary and Croatia, and about 2.1 million people live there.

The capital, Ljubljana, is a small city of pastel houses along a willow-lined river, with a hilltop castle above and a car-free center. Slovene, a Slavic language with a rare grammatical form used for exactly two of something, is the national language. Slovenia is a parliamentary republic and joined the European Union in 2004. More than half the country is covered in forest, one of the highest shares in Europe, and Slovenes are known for their beekeeping, their mountain huts, and cyclists who rank among the best in the world.
landAndNature: The Julian Alps fill the northwest, crowned by Mount Triglav at 2,864 meters, a three-headed peak that appears on the national flag; Slovenes joke that nobody is truly Slovene until they have climbed it. Beneath the southwest lies the Karst, a limestone plateau so famous that geographers everywhere borrow its name for landscapes of sinkholes, underground rivers and caves. Postojna Cave runs more than 24 kilometers and shelters the olm, a pale blind salamander that can live a century. Lake Bled reflects the Alps around a tiny island church. Brown bears, lynx and ibex still roam the forests and high slopes.
peopleAndCulture: Slovenes head for the mountains on weekends, and hiking is close to a national habit, with wardens serving soup in huts along the ridges. Bees matter here more than almost anywhere: Slovenia is known for painted beehive panels and persuaded the United Nations to declare World Bee Day on May 20, the birthday of the beekeeper Anton Janša. Food mixes Alpine, Italian and Balkan flavors, and potica, a rolled nut cake, is the festive favorite. Skiing and ski jumping fill winter television, and Slovenian riders have won the Tour de France. Culture Day on February 8 honors the poet France Prešeren, whose verses became the national anthem.
history: Celts and then Romans built towns here, including Emona, which lies beneath modern Ljubljana. Slavic ancestors of the Slovenes arrived in the 500s and formed the early duchy of Carantania. For more than 600 years the region was ruled by the Habsburgs from Vienna, which is why Austrian styles mark its churches and coffee houses. After World War I, Slovenia joined the kingdom that became Yugoslavia; it was occupied and divided during World War II, then returned to a communist-led Yugoslavia. In 1991 Slovenia declared independence, and the fighting that followed lasted only ten days, the briefest of the Yugoslav wars. Slovenia joined the European Union and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2007.
funFacts: The olm, a blind cave salamander found in Slovenia, can survive more than ten years without eating anything.
A small railway has carried visitors through Postojna Cave since 1872, one of the earliest underground train lines anywhere.
Ljubljana's symbol is a dragon, and four bronze dragons guard the corners of one bridge over the river.
About 60 percent of Slovenia is forest, making it one of the most densely wooded countries in Europe.
Roughly one in every 200 Slovenes keeps bees, and the country's campaign created the United Nations World Bee Day.
